case_study_insert.main_stem: Rio Sol Fruit Juices (RSFJ) is a public limited company in the fruit juice manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 240. Founded in 1991 by brothers Luis and Marco Herrera, the business bottles premium cold-pressed juice for national supermarkets and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership at head office. RSFJ plans to invest $1,850,000 in a new aseptic bottling plant, financed by a $1,100,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $510,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.10 a unit and a selling price of $7.50, and currently produces 210,000 units a year. RSFJ faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 16% among production staff and its warehouse reports a rising defect rate on capped bottles.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Market Research Summary — October 2026: A survey of 1,200 supermarket shoppers across five regions found that 61% prefer cold-pressed juice to from-concentrate, 55% would pay up to $0.80 more per bottle for premium juice, 49% associate the Rio Sol brand with freshness and 18% have bought juice through e-commerce in the past year. Weekly production is 4,300 units, and the defect rate is 1.5%, down from 2.7% a year ago. Average delivery lead time is 2.5 days. Customer complaints fell from 45 to 28 per month. 34 of 240 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new capping machines; off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Rio Sol Fruit Juices as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.5% to 6.25%, the fourth rise this year, increasing borrowing costs for businesses carrying variable-rate debt. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.0% from $13.00 to $13.91 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Orange, mango and guava input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, juice-price inflation is running at 9.3%, while consumer spending on premium beverages grew 5.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: RSFJ plans to finance part of its new aseptic bottling plant through a $1,100,000 share issue rather than bank borrowing. Explain two advantages for RSFJ of a share issue instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $1,100,000 with no obligation to repay or to pay fixed interest, which protects RSFJ's cash flow while it carries fixed costs of $510,000 a year and absorbs the 14.2% rise in orange, mango and guava costs. Debt service on an equivalent bank loan would add to the annual interest burden after the central bank's move to 6.25%, squeezing the margin above the $510,000 fixed base at exactly the moment RSFJ needs headroom to commission a $1,850,000 plant.

Point 2: Issuing shares spreads ownership and risk across new shareholders rather than concentrating it with a lender, and the $750,000 retained profit plus fresh equity avoids pledging the new aseptic line or existing plant as collateral. For a public limited company whose shares are already traded, accessing equity capital is a normal growth tool; it signals confidence to existing shareholders while leaving the board free to decide whether to pay dividends from future premium-juice profits rather than being locked into contractual interest. It also positions RSFJ to fund any later stage of the plant without renegotiating loan terms if premium-beverage demand, growing at 5.2%, accelerates.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Rio Sol Fruit Juices, its public limited status and its bottling plant expansion.

questions.question_text: RSFJ is launching its premium cold-pressed juice in new regions. Consider a national television campaign, in-store supermarket promotions, or social media influencer marketing. Which should RSFJ choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: Television would give RSFJ mass national reach very quickly, building awareness of the Rio Sol brand across every region it now supplies. It suits a public limited company with access to capital markets. However, production and airtime are extremely expensive, much of the audience neither drinks cold-pressed juice nor shops in RSFJ's supermarket partners, and the dilution of spend across hundreds of millions of non-target viewers would be hard for the board to justify while funding a $1,850,000 plant and absorbing 14.2% input-cost inflation.

In-store supermarket promotions: Point-of-sale tastings, shelf-edge pricing and loyalty card offers place the product directly in front of the buyers who already shop for juice. They are relatively cheap, measurable in units sold per store, and can push the 61% of shoppers who prefer cold-pressed to from-concentrate toward a first trial. Limitations are that promotions reach only existing footfall in listed stores, build little brand story beyond the aisle, and depend entirely on supermarket partners agreeing to display space and margin.

Social media influencer marketing: Food and health influencers can demonstrate freshness, premium quality and the $0.80 premium the 55% of surveyed shoppers will pay, targeting exactly the five regions in the market research with measurable engagement. It scales nationally at low cost per reached shopper, supports the 18% already buying via e-commerce, and lets RSFJ test creative before the full launch. Effectiveness is slower to compound and depends on influencer credibility, but the cost profile fits a company mid-expansion.

Recommendation: RSFJ should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by targeted in-store supermarket promotions at launch. Influencers reach the research-identified premium segment nationally and affordably, reinforcing freshness and justifying the $0.80 premium; television is rejected as wasteful and unaffordable against the plant investment and 14.2% input costs; in-store promotions alone are rejected as the primary strategy because they cannot build the brand story beyond existing shoppers or drive national trial quickly enough.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RSFJ with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RSFJ with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the television campaign and stand-alone in-store promotions are rejected.

questions.question_text: RSFJ operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. Explain two advantages for RSFJ of this structure and leadership style as it expands nationally.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership gives RSFJ a clear chain of command from head office to regional bottling and distribution teams, which speeds up decisions such as supermarket allocation, quality hold-ups on the capping line and responses to the 16% labour turnover problem. Senior leaders can impose uniform safety and hygiene standards across all sites without lengthy consultation, protecting national delivery lead times of 2.5 days and customer satisfaction with the declining complaint rate (45 to 28 per month).

Point 2: Autocratic direction is valuable during the commissioning of the new aseptic bottling plant, when RSFJ needs disciplined execution of capital works, staffing and supplier contracts across a 240-person workforce. Clear accountability and defined roles reduce confusion at shift handovers on the 4,300-unit weekly line, and experienced foremen can enforce the capping-machine training programme (34 staff outstanding) consistently. Predictable decision-making also reassures supermarket customers and the banks and shareholders funding the $1,850,000 plant that national expansion is being managed tightly rather than improvised.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RSFJ's national expansion, its 240-person workforce and its new plant.

questions.question_text: RSFJ needs 30 additional supervisors for the new aseptic bottling plant. Consider internal recruitment or external recruitment for these positions. Which should RSFJ choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Internal recruitment: Appointing supervisors from within RSFJ's 240 employees promotes experienced capping- and filling-line staff who already know the quality standards, the 1.5% defect rate target and the supermarket service culture. It motivates existing staff by showing career progression, shortens induction because internal candidates know RSFJ's systems, and is cheaper than advertising externally — important while funding a $1,850,000 plant. Drawbacks: internal promotion empties the skilled operator pool on the line, can entrench old habits that sit oddly with a new aseptic process, and may spark rivalry between equally experienced candidates, especially where hierarchy is rigid and leadership is autocratic.

External recruitment: Hiring 30 supervisors from outside brings fresh aseptic-process expertise from the wider food industry, wider talent choice, and new ideas on cutting the rising defect rate on capped bottles. It also avoids stripping experienced operators from the production floor during a sensitive ramp-up. However, external searches cost more in advertising, agency fees and longer induction, newcomers face cultural adjustment to RSFJ's hierarchical, autocratic style, and local labour turnover at 16% suggests onboarding must be strong to retain them.

Decision: RSFJ should choose internal recruitment for at least half the supervisor posts and external hires only for the specialised aseptic specialisms, then train the rest. Internal promotion is faster, cheaper and motivational during expansion, protects the line's existing quality culture, and fits the funds available after the share issue and retained profit commitment. External recruitment is rejected as the primary route because it costs more, learns more slowly against supermarket lead times of 2.5 days, and risks weakening RSFJ's proven 1.5% defect performance; where genuine aseptic expertise is absent in-house, a small number of external hires is justified as a complement, not a substitute.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of internal and external recruitment with limited application to RSFJ.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both recruitment options in the context of RSFJ's expansion.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both recruitment options in the context of RSFJ with a well-justified decision explaining why external recruitment is rejected as the primary route.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RSFJ's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $510,000 ÷ ($7.50 − $4.10) = $510,000 ÷ $3.40 = 150,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 150,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $7.50 − $4.10 = $3.40. Answer: contribution per unit is $3.40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RSFJ's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. RSFJ's managers can compare the 150,000-unit break-even output with current output of 210,000 units to confirm the business covers its $510,000 fixed costs with a margin of safety of 60,000 units, providing the headroom to fund the new bottling plant ramp-up without urgent price rises.
2. The contribution per unit of $3.40 lets managers test supermarket discounting: a 5% price cut to $7.13 would drop contribution to $3.03, so managers can see whether the volume gain from a promotion still covers fixed costs before accepting the supermarket's promotional terms.
3. Knowing break-even output lets managers set minimum order commitments in new-region supermarket listings, ensuring each region contributes toward the $510,000 fixed costs and the $1,850,000 plant's repayments before advertising spend is committed.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost (average total cost = $510,000 ÷ 210,000 units + $4.10 = $6.53 a unit) across quarters, identify whether the rising defect rate on capped bottles is inflating rework costs, and decide whether to pass part of the 14.2% input-cost inflation to supermarket customers or absorb it within the $3.40 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 150,000 units. Working: contribution per unit is $7.50 − $4.10 = $3.40, and $510,000 ÷ $3.40 = 150,000 units. (ii) Contribution per unit = $3.40. This is what each premium bottle contributes toward covering fixed costs after the fruit, bottle and cap costs are paid. (iii) Four contextual uses explained: First, RSFJ's managers can compare current output of 210,000 units with the 150,000-unit break-even to confirm a margin of safety of 60,000 units, giving the board confidence to commit to the new aseptic bottling plant without jeopardising the $750,000 retained profit cushion. Second, the $3.40 contribution lets managers model supermarket promotions precisely: a $0.40 promotional cut would leave $3.00 per unit, so RSFJ needs volumes above 170,000 units to keep total contribution above the $510,000 fixed costs — a concrete test of any promotion RSFJ is offered. Third, break-even analysis disciplines the regional rollout: each new supermarket region must commit to order volumes that push group output beyond 150,000 units before launch advertising is signed off, protecting the $1,850,000 plant investment. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($510,000 ÷ 210,000 units + $4.10 = $6.53 a unit) lets RSFJ track the effect of the 14.2% orange, mango and guava inflation, judge whether the rising defect rate on capped bottles is inflating rework costs, and decide when to pass costs into the $0.80 premium shoppers already accept.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RSFJ's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RSFJ's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.47 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $420,000 inventories + $520,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $1,030,000; 2025 current assets = $380,000 + $610,000 + $150,000 = $1,140,000. 2024 = $1,030,000 ÷ $700,000 = 1.47; 2025 = $1,140,000 ÷ $760,000 = 1.50. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($1,030,000 − $420,000) ÷ $700,000 = $610,000 ÷ $700,000 = 0.87; 2025 = ($1,140,000 − $380,000) ÷ $760,000 = $760,000 ÷ $760,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: RSFJ's liquidity has improved, though with a clear caveat. The slight rise from 1.47 to 1.50 shows current assets still cover current liabilities comfortably, and cash rose strongly from $90,000 to $150,000 after the share issue, strengthening short-term solvency during the plant build. The acid test moved from 0.87 to exactly 1.00, meaning RSFJ can now meet its current liabilities without selling a single bottle of juice — a meaningful milestone while it funds a $1,850,000 investment and services no new bank debt. However, trade receivables climbed from $520,000 to $610,000, soaking up $90,000 more cash with supermarket customers, which will reverse if they stretch terms; inventories fell from $420,000 to $380,000, so the ratio gains partly reflect liquidating stock rather than pure trading improvement.

Conclusion: RSFJ's financial position has improved — but modestly and with concentration risk. Both liquidity measures strengthened and the stock-independent measure reached parity, which is appropriate for a company mid-expansion. The warning sign is the rising trade receivables balance, so RSFJ should tighten supermarket credit control and monitor payment discipline while the new aseptic bottling plant comes on stream.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether RSFJ's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RSFJ of launching an e-commerce website for direct home delivery of its premium cold-pressed juice.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: An e-commerce website lets RSFJ sell directly to the 18% of shoppers who already buy juice online, capturing margin that supermarkets normally take and building first-party customer data for launching new flavours. It fits the premium positioning: the 55% willing to pay $0.80 more can subscribe for weekly deliveries, stabilising the 210,000-unit production schedule, improving cash flow through prepay, and creating a national channel independent of supermarket listing negotiations — helping repay the $1,850,000 plant investment faster. Direct feedback also sharpens market research beyond the periodic surveys.

Disadvantage: Building and running e-commerce adds significant operating costs — website development, payment systems, chilled last-mile delivery logistics and customer service — which can erode the $3.40 contribution per unit if basket sizes stay small. Chilled juice spoils quickly, so failed deliveries raise waste above the level the current 1.5% defect control assumes. Competing with supermarket prices online can also alienate retail partners RSFJ relies on for 210,000 units a year of volume, and RSFJ's 240-person workforce would need new skills in digital marketing and fulfilment that are scarce given the 16% labour turnover and 34 untrained capping-machine operators.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RSFJ's research data, distribution channels and expansion finances.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.25%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in orange, mango and guava input costs will affect RSFJ. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.5% to 6.25%): RSFJ funded the $1,850,000 plant with a $1,100,000 share issue and $750,000 retained profit, not bank debt, so the direct interest cost is limited to any existing variable-rate facilities. The 0.75% rise adds only a modest financing burden today, but raises the hurdle for future borrowing and can cool premium-beverage spending. It matters most for investor sentiment toward the public limited company's shares rather than for immediate cash flow.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $13.91 per hour from April 2026): With a workforce of 240 concentrated in bottling, packing and warehousing, wage costs are RSFJ's largest operating expense. If average pay rises from $13.00 to $13.91, each full-time employee costs roughly $1,800–$1,900 more a year, implying around $430,000–$460,000 of additional annual pay, before knock-on effects on salary differentials for the 30 planned supervisors. This is material but can be partly offset by the 1.5% defect-rate savings, automation in the new plant and productivity gains (210,000 units ÷ 240 staff ≈ 875 units per worker per year).

Input cost inflation (14.2% orange, mango and guava): Raw fruit dominates the $4.10 variable cost per unit. A 14.2% rise on the fruit component adds roughly $0.40–$0.55 per bottle; at 210,000 units that is about $84,000–$116,000 a year, dragging contribution from $3.40 toward $2.85–$3.00 and threatening the margin that the $7.50 premium price and $0.80 premium for eco-conscious buyers are designed to protect.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in orange, mango and guava input costs will have the greatest impact. It strikes every one of the 210,000 units sold each year, compounds with juice-price inflation at 9.3%, and directly squeezes the $3.40 contribution that funds the plant and dividends. The wage increase is the second most serious exposure, while the interest rate rise is least material because the expansion was equity-financed — but RSFJ must still defend margins through supplier contracts, hedging, pricing and efficiency across all three fronts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RSFJ.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RSFJ's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RSFJ with a well-justified judgement that the 14.2% input-cost rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
